drafts.title: $16,099 to let your EV power your house: GM V2G pilot in California
drafts.angle: The EV in the garage is turning into the biggest battery in the house, and now a utility pilot will help pay for it and pay you to use it. The next step for EV owners after solar.
bullets: GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid pilot with Southern California Edison customers (Electrek, Nov 19).
Eligible drivers can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system plus up to $8,099 toward installation through the California Energy Commission, over $16,000 total.
Drivers can be paid for taking part in demand-response events when the grid is tight; savings depend on rate plan and use.
Pilot covers Chevy, GMC and Cadillac EVs. GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities.
drafts.body: $16,099. That's the help California is offering some GM EV owners to let the car power the house and get paid when the grid is tight. My car sits parked {how many hours a day my car sits}. If your car could pay you back, would you hook it up to your house?
drafts.framework_body:
$16,099.

That's how much help some GM EV owners in California can get to let their car power the house. Up to $8,000 for the equipment and up to $8,099 for the install.

And when the grid gets tight on a hot afternoon, the utility pays you to send a little power back.

Most of us bought an EV to stop buying gas. Turns out the car is the biggest battery in the house. Mine sits parked {how many hours a day my car sits}.

My solar already covers {my monthly number}. If the car could keep the fridge and the furnace fan running during an outage and earn a few bucks on the side, that's not a science project. That's independence.

Right now it's a California pilot for Chevy, GMC and Cadillac owners. I want to see it come to Colorado.

If your car could pay you back, would you hook it up to your house?
drafts.ocr_why: Dollar opener, new 'your car pays you back' money angle for his most engaged EV audience, easy yes/no question.
drafts.pixel: Standing by your car and home charger: "My car sits here {hours} a day. What if it paid me back?"
drafts.premium_target: Quote Electrek's or Sawyer Merritt's post on the GM V2G pilot if one is up (none confirmed yet); one line: "The car is the biggest battery in the house. Pay me to use it."

drafts.title: California lets renters plug solar into a balcony outlet starting January
drafts.angle: Solar for people without a roof of their own. US angle only (Europe was covered elsewhere). Should Colorado copy it?
bullets: SB 868, the Plug and Play Solar Act, lets Californians install plug-in solar on balconies, railings, patios or ground stands starting January (NY Post, Nov 19).
One or two panels plus a microinverter, capped at 1,200 watts per home; must be UL or equivalent certified.
Landlords and HOAs still get a say; the exemption expires Jan 1, 2030.
Early online estimates put savings around $250 to $400 a year depending on sun and rates (estimates, not official).
Only two certified devices on the market so far, per Will Prowse as cited by NY Post.
drafts.body: $250 to $400 a year. That's what folks figure a balcony solar kit could save under California's new plug-in law, starting January. My roof makes {what my panels make on a sunny day}. Renters can't do that. Should Colorado let renters plug in?
drafts.framework_body:
$250 to $400 a year.

That's the rough savings people are figuring for a balcony solar kit under California's new plug-in solar law. It starts in January.

One or two panels on a railing or a patio, plugged into a regular outlet. Capped at 1,200 watts, has to be certified, and landlords and HOAs still get a say.

It won't run the house. But it chips away at the bill every single month.

I've got panels on my own roof and they make {what my panels make on a sunny day}. A lot of folks rent, or live in an apartment, and never get a piece of that.

{my take on renters and solar}.

Colorado has plenty of sun and plenty of renters. Should we let them plug in too?

drafts.title: Mesa County cuts the big-solar setback from 500 feet to 150
drafts.angle: His own county. Landowners and family farms vs neighbors. He's a rooftop solar owner here; keep it neighborly, not political.
bullets: Mesa County commissioners unanimously adopted a land development code overhaul on Tuesday, Nov 17 (KJCT, Nov 18).
Setback for large-scale solar from residential areas cut from a proposed 500 feet to 150 feet.
About 150 public comments came in; supporters said solar leases could help save a family farm.
Commissioner JJ Fletcher cited past solar companies not following permit conditions.
The code also drops the 180-day limit on living in an RV on your own property.
drafts.body: {$XX my panels saved me this year} on my own roof here in Mesa County. Commissioners just cut the setback for big solar farms from 500 feet to 150. Landowners say a solar lease can save a family farm. Fair to neighbors or not?
drafts.framework_body:
My panels saved me {$XX my panels saved me this year} on my own roof here in Mesa County.

This week our commissioners cut the setback for big solar farms. It was proposed at 500 feet from homes. Now it's 150.

About 150 people weighed in. Landowners said a solar lease can be the thing that keeps a family farm in the family. One commissioner pointed out that some solar companies haven't followed their permits in the past.

I'm a rooftop guy, so this isn't about me. It's about a farmer with land and bills, and a neighbor who wants a say in what goes up next door.

150 feet, plus companies that actually follow their permits, sounds like a fair middle to me. {my take}.

Neighbors, is 150 feet fair or not?
